{{Short description|Graphical representations of the variability of data}}
[[File:Confidenceinterval.png|thumb|A [[bar chart]] with [[confidence interval]]s (shown as red lines)]]

'''Error bars''' are graphical representations of the variability of data and used on graphs to indicate the [[Errors and residuals|error]] or [[Measurement uncertainty|uncertainty]] in a reported measurement. They give a general idea of how precise a measurement is, or conversely, how far from the reported value the true (error free) value might be. Error bars often represent one [[standard deviation]] of uncertainty, one [[standard error]], or a particular [[confidence interval]] (e.g., a 95% interval).  These quantities are not the same and so the measure selected should be stated explicitly in the graph or supporting text.

Error bars can be used to compare visually two quantities if various other conditions hold.  This can determine whether differences are [[statistically significant]].  Error bars can also suggest [[goodness of fit]] of a given function, i.e., how well the function describes the data.  Scientific papers in the experimental sciences are expected to include error bars on all graphs, though the practice differs somewhat between sciences, and each journal will have its own [[Style guide|house style]]. It has also been shown that error bars can be used as a [[direct manipulation interface]] for controlling probabilistic algorithms for approximate computation.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sarkar|first1=Advait|last2=Blackwell|first2=Alan F.|last3=Jamnik|first3=Mateja|last4=Spott|first4=Martin |url=https://advait.org/files/sarkar_2015_uncertainty_vis.pdf |doi=10.2312/eurovisshort.20151138|year=2015|journal=Eurographics Conference on Visualization (Eurovis) - Short Papers|title=Interaction with Uncertainty in Visualisations}}</ref> Error bars can also be expressed in a [[plus–minus sign]] (±), plus the upper limit of the error and minus the lower limit of the error.<ref name="stderror">{{cite journal|title=Standard Deviation, Standard Error: Which 'Standard' Should We Use?|first=George W.|last=Brown|journal=American Journal of Diseases of Children|year=1982|volume=136|issue=10|pages=937–941|doi=10.1001/archpedi.1982.03970460067015|pmid=7124681}}.</ref>

A notorious misconception in elementary statistics is that error bars show whether a statistically significant difference exists, by checking simply for whether the error bars overlap; this is not the case.<ref name="Error bars in experimental biology">{{cite journal|last1=Cumming|first1=Geoff|last2=Fidler|first2=Fiona|author-link2=Fiona Fidler|last3=Vaux|first3=David L.|title=Error bars in experimental biology|journal=The Journal of Cell Biology|date=9 April 2007|volume=177|issue=1|pages=7–11|doi=10.1083/jcb.200611141|pmid=17420288|pmc=2064100}}</ref><ref name="The (mis)use of overlap of confidence intervals to assess effect modification">{{cite journal|last1=Knol|first1=Mirjam J.|last2=Pestman|first2=Wiebe R.|last3=Grobbee|first3=Diederick E.|title=The (mis)use of overlap of confidence intervals to assess effect modification|journal=European Journal of Epidemiology|date=19 March 2011|volume=26|issue=4|pages=253–254|doi=10.1007/s10654-011-9563-8|pmid=21424218|pmc=3088813}}</ref><ref name="Researchers misunderstand confidence intervals and standard error bars">{{cite journal|last1=Belia|first1=Sarah|last2=Fidler|first2=Fiona|last3=Williams|first3=Jennifer|last4=Cumming|first4=Geoff|title=Researchers misunderstand confidence intervals and standard error bars|journal=Psychological Methods|date=2005|volume=10|issue=4|pages=389–396|doi=10.1037/1082-989X.10.4.389|pmid=16392994}}</ref>
